Format your results in the following way: Start : Tag1 End : Tag1 Start : Tag2 -> Attribute2[0] > Attribute_value2[0] -> Attribute2[1] > Attribute_value2[1] -> Attribute2[2] > Attribute_value2[2] Start : Tag3 -> Attribute3[0] > None Empty : Tag4 -> Attribute4[0] > Attribute_value4[0] End : Tag3 End : Tag2 Here, the -> symbol indicates that the tag contains an attribute. It is immediately followed by the name of the attribute and the attribute value. The > symbol acts as a separator of the attribute and the attribute value. def get_note(pitch):
```python
    notes_dictionary = {
        440: "A",
        466.16: "A#",
        493.88: "B",
        523.25: "C",
        554.37: "C#", 
        587.33: "D", 
        622.25: "D#", 
        659.25: "E", 
        698.46: "F", 
        739.99: "F#", 
        783.99: "G", 
        830.61: "G#"
    }
    
    for frequency, note in notes_dictionary.items():
        ratio = pitch / frequency
        if ratio == 1 or abs(ratio - 2) < 1e-5 or abs(ratio - 0.5) < 1e-5:
            return note
```

Solve the following programming problem. Implement the requested callable `get_note` exactly as specified. Return only complete Python code in one ```python code block, with no explanation.

Problem:
In music, if you double (or halve) the pitch of any note you will get to the same note again.

"Concert A" is fixed at 440 Hz, and every other note is defined based on that. 880 Hz is also an A, as is 1760 Hz, as is 220 Hz.

There are 12 notes in Western music: A, A#, B, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#. You are given a preloaded dictionary with these 12 notes and one of the pitches that creates that note (starting at Concert A).

Now, given a pitch (in Hz), return the corresponding note. (All inputs will be valid notes).

For reference, the notes dictionary looks like this:

```python

    440: "A",
    466.16: "A#",
    493.88: "B",

    622.25: "D#", 
    659.25: "E", 
    698.46: "F", 
    739.99: "F#", 
    783.99: "G", 
    830.61: "G#"
}
```
